Should Students Take a Gap Year?

After finishing high school, many students feel pressure to go straight to university. But I believe a gap year can be a good idea if students plan it carefully.

One big benefit is that it helps students figure out what they want. Many of my classmates are choosing a major just because it sounds respectable or because their parents suggested it. A year of working or volunteering could show them what they actually enjoy. Students who take that time often come back more focused and motivated.

A gap year also teaches real-life skills. Working a job, saving money, or traveling alone helps you become more independent and responsible. These are things you cannot learn from a textbook, and universities and employers like to see them.

On the other hand, a gap year has risks. It can cost a lot of money, and some students may get out of the habit of studying. If a student has no plan, the year might just be wasted watching videos and sleeping late.

Overall, I think a gap year is a good idea for students who have clear goals, like earning money, learning a skill, or gaining experience. For students who already know what they want, going straight to university is fine. The important thing is to make a choice on purpose.

The man at the corner table had been typing for almost an hour, and Priya had been watching him for most of it.

It wasn't a creepy kind of watching, she told herself. She had finished her book, her latte had gone cold, and he was simply the most interesting thing in the room. He hunched over his laptop like someone defusing a bomb. Every few minutes he stopped, stared at the ceiling, and then went back to it with a small, satisfied nod.

Outside, the afternoon was bright and hard, the kind of cloudless sky that makes people squint and complain about the heat. A bus sighed past the window. A kid on a scooter wobbled down the sidewalk.

The man leaned forward. Priya, who had slid her chair a little sideways for a better view, could see the screen over his shoulder. A cursor blinked in a wall of text. He typed slowly, one letter at a time, as if he wanted to enjoy it.

*It begins raining outside.*

He hit the period. He sat back.

For a second, nothing. Then the light in the window changed, a gray shadow sliding over the street. The first drops struck the glass, fat and scattered. Within moments the scooter kid was gone and people on the sidewalk were running, holding bags and newspapers over their heads. The rain came down in sheets, loud on the awning, and the whole café seemed to exhale.

Priya realized she was holding her breath.

"Coincidence," she whispered. But the sky had been perfectly clear. She'd checked her phone ten minutes ago. Sunny, ninety-one degrees, zero percent chance.

The man didn't look surprised. He looked tired. He rubbed his eyes, glanced at the window, and typed something else. Priya couldn't read it from where she sat, but a moment later the rain softened into a gentle drizzle.

She stood up before she could think better of it and walked over. "Excuse me."

He looked up. He was older than she'd expected, maybe sixty, with kind, crumpled eyes. "Yes?"

"I saw what you wrote. Before it rained."

"Ah." He closed the laptop halfway. "You're very observant."

"Did you do that?"

He smiled, a little sadly. "I'm a novelist. Or I was. I've been stuck on the same chapter for two years. This morning I started writing small things, simple things, just to remember how it felt." He shrugged. "The weather seemed harmless."

"Harmless," Priya repeated. "You made it rain."

"I wrote that it rained. I'm not sure those are the same."

She looked at the laptop. Then she looked at him. "Can I ask you to try something?"

"That depends."

"My sister's flight lands in an hour. She's terrified of turbulence."

The man laughed, a real laugh, startling in the quiet café. He opened the laptop fully, flexed his fingers, and waited.

"Tell me about her," he said.

Many people say that money is the key to happiness, while others believe happiness comes from something else. I think that money helps, but it is not the most important thing.

Money can make life easier. If a family has enough to pay for food, a safe home, and health care, they have fewer worries. Imagine a student who has to work late every night just to help pay the bills. That student has little time to rest, study, or enjoy being young. In this way, money gives people freedom and security, and that can make them happier.

However, having a lot of money does not guarantee happiness. There are many rich people who feel lonely or stressed. They may spend all their time working and have no time for their family or friends. On the other hand, some people have very little money but still smile every day because they have people who love them and activities they enjoy. My grandmother, for example, never had much money, but she was one of the happiest people I ever met because she was always surrounded by family and neighbors.

In my opinion, happiness comes mostly from good relationships, health, and having goals that matter to you. Money is useful, but it is only a tool. If we depend on it too much, we may forget about the things that really make life meaningful.

Ghosts take our things because they have nothing else to hold on to.

I learned this the winter after my grandmother died, when the house on Pell Street started eating my keys. Not once, but every day, always in the same place, the blue bowl by the door. I would set them down and a minute later they were gone. At first I blamed myself. Then my coffee mug disappeared from the counter. A single earring. My reading glasses, which I found a week later on the kitchen windowsill, folded neatly, facing the street.

My brother Dev thought I was losing my mind. "Grief does that," he said. But Dev's sunglasses vanished the next weekend, and after that he stopped saying it.

I started leaving things out on purpose. A spoon. A button. A pencil. I would come back to find them moved, never gone, always arranged somewhere new. The spoon on the stairs. The button on the piano. The pencil lined up on the sill beside my glasses.

On a night when I couldn't sleep, I sat in the dark kitchen and put down a small thing, my grandmother's thimble, and waited. I held my breath. The air got cold in the way it does just before snow, and the thimble slid across the table, slowly, a few inches at a time, until it reached the edge of the window where the light from the street came in.

That was when I understood. My grandmother used to sit at that window every evening, watching the street, waiting for people to come home. She had never been good at saying she missed us. She kept the porch light on. She counted the cars.

The things were not being taken. They were being collected. Each object was a small piece of someone who had lived there: my keys, the glasses, a mug that still smelled of my coffee. They were evidence that the house was still full. A ghost has no hands to hold a person. It has only the things people leave behind.

So I stopped hiding my keys. I stopped asking for them back, too. The next morning I set a fresh cup of tea beside the thimble and said, out loud, "I'm still here, Grandma."

The cup was empty by evening.

Months later, when I finally sold the house, I walked through the rooms with the new owners, a young couple with a baby. I did not warn them. I only said that if they ever lost something small, they should not worry too much. It would turn up on the windowsill.

I left the blue bowl by the door.

Tourism is good and bad for local people. I think the benefits are bigger than the problems, but not always.

First, tourism gives many jobs. Tourists need hotels, restaurants and guides, so local people can find work and earn money. In my city, many families have small shops because tourists come every summer. Also, the money can help to build better roads and buildings.

But tourism has some problems too. Sometimes the places are too crowded and noisy. Prices can become more high, and local people cannot afford to live there. Tourists also leave a lot of trash in the nature.

In my opinion, the government must make rules to protect the places and the people. If they do this, tourism can be very useful for everyone. So, I think the benefits are more important.

Waking up fresh mostly comes down to what you do in the 24 hours before, not what happens when the alarm goes off. A few things make the biggest difference.

**Keep a consistent schedule.** Going to bed and waking up at about the same time every day, even on weekends, trains your body clock. This is probably the single most effective habit. If your wake time shifts by two or three hours on weekends, you give yourself a kind of mini jet lag every Monday.

**Get enough sleep.** Most adults need seven to nine hours. Work backward from your wake-up time to figure out when you actually need to be asleep, and be honest about how long it takes you to fall asleep.

**Wind down properly.** Dim the lights an hour before bed, put your phone away or at least switch off notifications, and avoid heavy meals, alcohol, and caffeine in the late afternoon and evening. A cool, dark, quiet room helps a lot.

**Wake up in light.** Light is the strongest signal telling your brain it's morning. Open the curtains right away, or step outside for a few minutes. If you wake before sunrise, a bright lamp or a sunrise-simulating alarm can help.

**Don't hit snooze.** Fragmented sleep after the first alarm is low quality and often makes grogginess worse. Put the alarm across the room so you have to get up, or set it for the time you really need to wake.

**Move and hydrate.** A glass of water and a bit of movement, such as stretching or a short walk, get your blood flowing. Eating a reasonable breakfast can help too, though it matters less than the rest.

Be patient with yourself. If you change your habits, it can take a week or two to feel the difference. If you sleep enough and still feel exhausted every morning, it's worth talking to a doctor, since conditions like sleep apnea or thyroid problems can cause it.

The Scheveningen (1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3 d6) is a flexible Sicilian setup where Black keeps a compact pawn structure with pawns on d6 and e6 and delays committing the pieces. White has several well-established plans, and which one you choose usually depends on your style.

**The English Attack (Be3, f3, Qd2, O-O-O, g4).** Currently the most popular and dangerous approach. White castles queenside and launches a pawn storm with g4-g5 against Black's kingside. Black typically counters with ...a6, ...b5, and ...Bb7 or ...Nbd7, aiming for queenside play and central breaks like ...d5. The race is sharp, so knowledge of theory matters.

**The Classical setup (Be2, O-O, f4, Kh1, Be3, Qe1 or Qd2).** White castles short and builds up slowly, with f4 and sometimes a4, preparing e5 or a kingside attack. This is a more strategic approach and gives White a solid position, although Black has plenty of counterplay.

**The Keres Attack (g4).** After 6.g4, White immediately threatens g5 to drive away the f6 knight. This was Paul Keres's invention and remains a serious weapon. Black usually replies with ...h6 or ...Nc6 and aims to strike back with ...d5 or ...Nxd4 followed by ...e5.

**The Sozin Attack (Bc4 and Be3).** White develops the bishop actively to c4, often followed by castling kingside or queenside depending on Black's setup. It can lead to sharp positions where Black has to be careful about the pressure against e6.

**The Fischer plan (Bc4 with Qe2, 0-0-0).** Not a different line so much as a variation of the above, but Fischer's handling of it, with Black's king getting pressured on the d-file, is a classic model.

**The Maroczy-style and quiet setups (Be2, a4, and Be3).** White restricts Black's queenside expansion by playing a4 to stop ...b5, then plays slowly with f4 and Bf3 or Qd2 and O-O-O, aiming for a small, steady advantage.

Some general ideas run through all of these lines. White usually wants to exploit the extra space in the center, keep the d4 knight well placed, watch for sacrifices on e6 or the pawn break e4-e5, and aim at the weaknesses on d6 and e6. Black, meanwhile, aims for ...d5 to equalize, queenside expansion with ...b5, and counterattack against White's king if White castles long.

If you want to get started, the English Attack is great for aggressive players, while the Classical system with Be2 suits people who prefer a more solid, strategic game.

# The Roman Republic and the Roman Empire

## The Roman Republic (509-27 BCE)

**Origins.** According to tradition, Rome was founded in 753 BCE and ruled by kings. In 509 BCE the Romans expelled the last king, Tarquin the Proud, and set up a republic. Power was shared among elected magistrates (two consuls chosen each year), the Senate (an advisory body of aristocrats), and popular assemblies.

**Social conflict.** Early Republican history was shaped by the "Conflict of the Orders," in which plebeians (commoners) pushed for political rights against the patrician elite. Over about two centuries they won the right to hold office, protection through tribunes, and, in 450 BCE, a written law code, the Twelve Tables.

**Expansion.** Rome gradually conquered the Italian peninsula, binding defeated peoples to it through alliances and partial citizenship. It then fought three Punic Wars against Carthage (264-146 BCE). Hannibal's invasion of Italy nearly broke Rome, but Rome won and destroyed Carthage in 146 BCE. In the same period, Rome took control of Greece, Spain, and much of the eastern Mediterranean.

**Crisis.** Conquest brought wealth, slaves, and inequality. Small farmers lost their land, and ambitious generals gained armies loyal to themselves rather than the state. The Gracchi brothers' reform attempts (133-121 BCE) ended in violence, and the first century BCE was marked by civil wars involving Marius and Sulla, then Pompey and Julius Caesar. Caesar crossed the Rubicon in 49 BCE, won the civil war, and was assassinated in 44 BCE. A further round of conflict ended when Octavian defeated Mark Antony and Cleopatra at Actium in 31 BCE.

## The Roman Empire (27 BCE-476 CE in the West)

**The Principate.** In 27 BCE the Senate gave Octavian the title Augustus. He kept republican forms but held real power himself, effectively becoming the first emperor. His reign began the *Pax Romana*, roughly two centuries of relative peace and prosperity across the Mediterranean world.

**Peak and growth.** Under emperors such as Trajan (r. 98-117 CE), the empire reached its greatest extent, stretching from Britain to Mesopotamia and containing perhaps 50 to 70 million people. Trade, cities, and roads flourished.

**Crisis and reform.** The third century brought civil war, plague, economic trouble, and invasions. Diocletian (r. 284-305) restored order by dividing administration between East and West. Constantine (r. 306-337) legalized Christianity, which later became the state religion, and founded Constantinople as a new capital.

**Decline.** The Western Empire faced migrations and invasions by Goths, Vandals, and others, and its last emperor, Romulus Augustulus, was deposed in 476 CE. The Eastern Empire, usually called the Byzantine Empire, lasted until the Ottomans captured Constantinople in 1453.

## Key achievements

- **Law and government.** Roman law, from the Twelve Tables to Justinian's codification, shaped legal systems across Europe and beyond. Ideas such as written statutes, legal personhood, and the presumption of innocence have Roman roots. The Republic's mixed constitution also influenced modern political thinkers and the framers of the U.S. Constitution.
- **Engineering and architecture.** Romans built roads, aqueducts, bridges, and public baths, and they made extensive use of the arch, the vault, and concrete. The Pantheon's dome and the Colosseum still stand.
- **Military organization.** The professional legions, with their discipline, logistics, and engineering skills, were among the most effective fighting forces of the ancient world.
- **Language and literature.** Latin evolved into the Romance languages and supplied vocabulary to many others. Writers such as Cicero, Virgil, Livy, and Tacitus left works that remain central to Western literature.
- **Integration and administration.** Rome extended citizenship over time, ran provincial administration, and linked a vast territory through trade and a shared urban culture.
- **Cultural transmission.** Romans preserved and spread Greek philosophy, art, and science, and the empire's later embrace of Christianity helped shape medieval Europe.

For an assignment, it may help to choose one angle, such as why the Republic collapsed or how Augustus consolidated power, and develop it with primary sources like Polybius, Livy, Suetonius, or Augustus' own *Res Gestae*.

# Iran's Supreme Leader Weighs Legacy as Memory of Khomeini's Painful Peace Lingers

When Iran's first Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, agreed to end the long war with Saddam Hussein's Iraq, he did so reluctantly. He described the decision as bitter, a concession that many in Iran found hard to accept after years of fighting and enormous loss.

More than two decades later, that moment is being revisited as Iran's current Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, faces questions about his own legacy.

Nazila Fathi, a journalist who has covered Iran for years, asks whether Khamenei is trying to put the country on the right track before he dies. Her question speaks to a wider debate inside and outside Iran about how the aging leader will be remembered and what direction the Islamic Republic will take after him.

Khomeini's peace with Iraq stands as one of the most consequential choices of the revolutionary era. Having led his country through a grueling war, he ultimately chose to stop it, even though doing so required him to set aside his own deeply held positions. The comparison is notable because it shows a leader willing to accept a painful compromise for the sake of the country's future.

Whether Khamenei is considering a similar change of course is unclear. Supporters of the government would likely say that he has guided Iran steadily through years of pressure. Critics say the country faces serious economic and political challenges that call for a different approach.

Fathi suggests that the leader's age and place in history may be shaping his choices. If so, the coming months could show whether he intends to leave behind a government that has made peace with its adversaries, or one that holds to the same path.

Either way, the shadow of Khomeini's bitter peace continues to hang over the decisions made in Tehran today.

**Pentagon Map Suggests Coalition Has Retaken Up to 30 Percent of Iraqi Territory From ISIS**

The Pentagon has released a map indicating that coalition and Iraqi forces have regained between 25 and 30 percent of the territory in Iraq that was once held by the extremist group ISIS, according to defense officials.

The map, which marks areas formerly under militant control, is intended to illustrate the progress of the campaign against the group since airstrikes and ground operations intensified. Officials said the figures reflect a reduction in the amount of populated territory that ISIS is able to hold and administer.

Analysts cautioned, however, that territory alone does not provide a full picture of the conflict. Afzal Ashraf, a counterinsurgency specialist, said the new data should be read carefully and in context.

"The map tells us something important, but it does not tell us everything," Ashraf said. He noted that ISIS has adapted its tactics in response to coalition air power, avoiding large, exposed formations that can be targeted from above.

"Where it counts, they are not standing and fighting," Ashraf said. "They are melting away, regrouping, and choosing when and where to engage."

According to Ashraf, this approach means that recapturing ground does not necessarily equate to destroying the group's fighting capacity. Militants who withdraw from one area may reappear elsewhere, and they can continue to rely on ambushes, improvised explosive devices, and attacks on soft targets.

He added that holding territory, once it has been retaken, presents its own challenge. Local security forces must be capable of preventing a return of insurgents, and local populations must be convinced that the government can protect them and provide basic services.

Defense officials have said they expect the campaign to be long and have emphasized the role of training and equipping Iraqi forces. The Pentagon has not provided a timeline for further operations.

Ashraf said that observers should look at additional indicators, including the group's financial resources, its ability to recruit, and the stability of areas that have been cleared, in order to measure genuine progress against the organization.
